title: Near-Field Characterisation of Guided Modes in WS2 Nanobeams and Quasi-Bulk Crystals
authors: Zara S. Taylor, Luke M. Hallacy, Xuerong Hu, Oliver T. Williams, Simone Strohmair, Fabian Felixberger, Alexander J. Knight, Timothy Chester-Parsons, Luke R. Wilson, Alexander I. Tartakovskii
abstract: The exceptionally high in-plane refractive index, low sub-bandgap absorption, and strong optical anisotropy of WS2 make it a promising material platform for next-generation integrated circuits for nanophotonics. Its layered van der Waals structure further enables heterogeneous integration with silicon photonics and emerging two-dimensional optoelectronic materials. However, despite increasing interest in the waveguiding properties of WS2, experimental studies of wavelength-dependent modal confinement and attenuation remain limited. Additionally, though the extinction coefficient of WS2 is expected to be near-negligible beneath the bandgap, reported values span orders of magnitude, leading to large uncertainty in predicted modal decay lengths and wafer-scale integration feasibility. To resolve these ambiguities we perform hyperspectral cavity-enhanced imaging, determining high-resolution upper and lower bounds on the extinction coefficient of WS2 within the visible-NIR edge. We further employ scattering-type scanning near-field optical microscopy (s-SNOM) to probe TE0, TM0, and higher-order modes in both quasi-bulk and nanobeam WS2 waveguides across the 800-1400 nm spectral range, enabling identification of mode-specific trends in wavevector dispersion and loss. This work simultaneously assesses s-SNOM as a probe of waveguide performance, and we find that while absolute loss values depend on measurement geometry, s-SNOM reliably captures relative modal trends and provides upper bounds on propagation loss, supporting its use as a diagnostic tool for anisotropic waveguides. We further identify significant artefacts in nanobeam measurements arising from transverse interference and spatial sampling effects when the structure size approaches the excitation wavelength, which can shift extracted effective indices by up to 0.25.
summary: This work characterizes the guided optical modes in WS2 nanobeams and quasi-bulk crystals using both near-field microscopy (s-SNOM) and cavity spectroscopy (iCEAS). The authors establish that s-SNOM is a robust tool for measuring relative modal dispersion across visible-NIR wavelengths, while also quantifying material absorption to improve the feasibility of integrating these 2D materials into photonic circuits.
main_problem: The study addresses the limited experimental understanding of wavelength-dependent modal confinement and attenuation in WS2 waveguides, complicated by ambiguities in material extinction coefficient values.
main_result: s-SNOM reliably captures relative modal trends for TE0 and TM0 modes across 800–1400 nm, confirming its utility as a diagnostic tool despite absolute loss dependence on measurement geometry.
method: The authors employed hyperspectral cavity-enhanced imaging (iCEAS) to constrain material absorption and utilized scattering-type s-SNOM microscopy to probe guided modes in quasi-bulk and nanobeam WS2 waveguides.
model_or_system: The physical system is WS2, a layered van der Waals semiconductor promising for nanophotonics due to its high refractive index and anisotropy. The analysis involves modeling TE0 and TM0 modes using Lumerical FDE simulations alongside experimental measurements on patterned nanobeams and bulk flakes.
key_observables: Effective indices (neff), modal confinement, propagation loss ($	ext{dB}/	ext{mm}$), birefringence ($\Delta n$), and the extinction coefficient ($\kappa$).
important_parameters: Wavelength range of 800–1400 nm; waveguide thicknesses around 112 nm to 200 nm; nanobeam widths from 400 nm to 650 nm.
main_assumptions: Absolute propagation losses measured by s-SNOM are influenced by measurement geometry and coupling factors, requiring relative trend analysis. Artifacts due to transverse interference in narrow beams must be accounted for.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate atomic structure, simulated effective index maps for TE0/TM0 modes, s-SNOM images showing fringe patterns across varying wavelengths, and plots correlating extracted neff and decay constants with mode filling factor or waveguide width.
paper_structure: The paper systematically moves from characterizing the material properties (absorption via iCEAS) to simulating ideal modal behavior (FDE simulations), and finally performing detailed near-field measurements using s-SNOM on both quasi-bulk crystals and patterned nanobeams, analyzing mode dispersion and leakage effects.
why_interesting: The rigorous application of advanced optical characterization techniques like s-SNOM and iCEAS to a 2D material platform provides crucial experimental benchmarks for designing next-generation integrated photonic circuits.
